## Why

On a repo where Entire has no readable checkpoints, `brain refresh` (also `refresh sessions`, `refresh delta`) hard-failed with egress allowed:

while the same repo under `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS=1` succeeded with a friendly "no checkpoints have been captured" warning. The failure also made `doctor`'s remedy circular: it pointed at setup, whose first stage is the export that just failed.

Fixes [COR-2203](https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/COR-2203).

## What changed

- `discoverCheckpoints` (internal/cli/export.go): an incomplete inventory with zero readable IDs now returns the empty result with warnings (the scope-incomplete note plus the no-checkpoints-yet notice), matching the no-egress path, instead of erroring.

## Safety

A populated brain cannot be silently emptied by this: `runExport`'s empty-export refusal still rejects replacing a brain that already holds sessions. The setup/status no-sessions hint machinery stays, because brains set up by older binaries still carry the recorded failure detail.

- `go test ./internal/cli/` passes (full package).

COR-2203 is fixed and in review: https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/428 (ticket moved to In Review with the PR linked).

- **Fix**: `discoverCheckpoints` (`internal/cli/export.go:944`) no longer hard-fails when Entire reports an incomplete inventory with zero readable checkpoint IDs. It now returns the empty result with warnings (scope-incomplete note + "no checkpoints have been captured yet"), matching the no-egress path. This also removes the circular `doctor` → `setup` → same-failure loop.
- **Safety**: a populated brain cannot be silently emptied — `runExport`'s empty-export refusal (`export.go:295`) still rejects replacing a brain that already holds sessions. The setup/status no-sessions hint machinery stays, since brains set up by older binaries persist the old failure string.

- **Validation**: full `go test ./internal/cli/` passes (one test, `TestEgressAllowedNoSessionsIsNotSentBackToRefresh`, pinned the old fail-honestly behavior and was rewritten to pin the new agreement); `gofmt -l -s` clean. Note: no `oxfmt` exists in this repo or on PATH — CI's lint step is `gofmt -l -s`, which I ran instead.

content.text:
COR-2203 validated on main and closed.

- **Built from main** (`1e28fbd2`, the PR #428 merge) and ran the ticket's repro on a fresh never-checkpointed repo.
- **Exact ticket state** (incomplete scope + zero readable IDs, forced via a stub `entire` binary): `refresh sessions` now exits 0 with "exported 0 sessions from 0 checkpoints", the plainly worded scope warning, and the "no checkpoints have been captured yet" notice — identical outcome to `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS=1` on the same repo.

- One observation: with the real host CLI this scratch repo reported a *complete* empty inventory (a different, already-working path) — the incomplete-scope path needed the stub to reproduce, and it's pinned by the two new unit tests.
- Ticket moved to Done with the validation evidence as a comment; scratch repo, binary, and its brain dir cleaned up.

input.message:
Cursor Bugbot flagged a real issue on your PR #436 (internal/cli/add.go:110-121, cloneFailureMessage) — please fix it on the same branch.

Finding (Medium): the classifier treats ANY stderr containing "correct access rights" or "permission denied" as "repository not found (or no access)". But git appends the "Please make sure you have the correct access rights and the repository exists." footer to most SSH transport failures (host key verification failed, connection refused/timed out), and "Permission denied" also appears for local failures like "fatal: could not create work tree dir ...: Permission denied". Those collapse into the not-found line and hide the real cause.

Fix direction:
- Narrow the classification. Keep "repository not found (or no access)" only for genuine repo-missing/auth-denied signals: e.g. "repository ... not found" / "Repository not found", and SSH auth specifically ("Permission denied (publickey" form), not bare "permission denied" and not the "correct access rights" footer at all.
- Everything else (host key verification failed, could not resolve hostname, connection refused/timed out, local permission-denied creating the worktree) should fall through to your existing generic fallback that surfaces the de-duplicated meaningful stderr line — prefer the most specific fatal/error line over the generic footer when both are present.
- Extend TestRunBrainAddCloneFailureIsOneCleanLine with cases: host-key-verification-failed stderr (must show that line, not not-found), connection refused/timeout, local "could not create work tree dir: Permission denied" (must show the real line), and keep the SSH "Permission denied (publickey)." case mapping to no-access.

Workflow: same branch cor-2206-add-clone-errors in your worktree; run gofmt -l -s on changed files and the focused add tests (full suite not needed again for this — it's string classification only, but run `go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'BrainAdd|Clone' -count=1`); commit with explicit file names ending with the same Co-Authored-By line; push. Then reply on the PR to the bugbot thread briefly stating what changed (one or two sentences, cold-reader style) — you can use `gh pr comment 436 --body ...`. Report back: the new classifier rules, test cases added, and confirmation of push + comment.

CI is failing on your PR #433: benchmark-corpus job, module benchmarks/agent-brain/test_publication_safety.py. Root cause diagnosed — fix it on the same branch (cor-2207-connect-placement-error).

Cause: that test bans publication-unsafe identifiers in tracked files, including the regex for internal auth endpoints `\b(?:us|eu)\.auth\.entire\.io\b`. Your new test fixture in internal/cli/connect_cmd_test.go pins the ticket's repro stderr verbatim, which contains `Using context 'us.auth.entire.io'.` — a banned string.

Fix: replace the hostname in your test fixture(s) with a fake one, e.g. `Using context 'auth.example.invalid'.` — your banner-stripping matches the `Using context ` prefix, not the hostname, so the test loses nothing. Check the whole diff for any other occurrence of `us.auth.entire.io` or other banned identifiers (run `python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/test_publication_safety.py` locally to verify it passes — it only scans tracked files, so commit first or check against your working tree accordingly).

Then: gofmt, run the focused connect tests plus `python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/test_publication_safety.py`, commit (explicit file names, same Co-Authored-By line), push. Also note PR #433 has an "Entire Gates" check failure (https://entire.com/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/344) — after pushing, check whether the gate re-runs/clears; if it reports something unrelated to the publication-safety string, report what it says rather than chasing it.

Bugbot re-reviewed PR #436 at head f4b60d09 (note: main was merged into your branch meanwhile): your first fix cleared, but it found one new Medium issue in cloneFailureMessage (internal/cli/add.go:120) — fix on the same branch.

Finding: "Clone classifier matches tokens across lines." `strings.Contains(lower, "repository") && strings.Contains(lower, "not found")` tests the WHOLE stderr, not a single line. Example: a remote missing git-upload-pack prints `bash: git-upload-pack: command not found` plus git's `fatal: Could not read from remote repository.` footer — "not found" from one line + "repository" from another → misclassified as "repository not found (or no access)", hiding the real PATH/install cause.

Fix: evaluate the not-found signal per line — classify only when a single line contains both "repository" and "not found" (git's `fatal: repository '<url>' not found` and GitHub's `remote: Repository not found.` both satisfy that). Keep the other auth signals as-is (they're single-phrase matches and safe). Add a test case: the git-upload-pack-missing stderr above must surface the `command not found` cause line, not the not-found classification; keep the existing not-found cases green.

content.text:
**What it is** — `local-gitmeta` is the default storage backend for `memories sync` (the durable facts/memories set). It's a bare git repository on your disk at `<cache>/brain/<repo-key>/gitmeta.git` with a single local ref (`refs/meta/local/main`), no remote. Per branch it stores two "git-meta" records: a **head** key (`<version>|<contentRef>`, advanced by compare-and-swap) and a **blob** key holding the full NDJSON fact set. Each sync overwrites the one blob key, so live state stays O(1) while prior versions remain in git history.

**Why it's used** (from the package docs and recorded Brain memories):

1. **Same seam as hosted, zero infrastructure.** It implements the identical `factsync.Server` interface as the hosted HTTP backend — same content-addressed refs and CAS semantics (`ErrConflict` on a lost swap, `ErrNoChange` on an identical blob). One sync/merge engine works both offline and hosted; git-meta is literally "the offline sibling of factsync.HTTPServer" with no entire-api, entiredb, Postgres, or mTLS.
2. **No-implicit-egress model (ADR-P1-A).** A plain `memories sync` never leaves the machine; hosted is opt-in via `--memories-backend=http`. That's the COR-2211 default you have the open decision on.
3. **Durability + concurrency safety for free.** Git refs plus a filesystem lock give atomic CAS and versioned history without running any service.

**Why it's local-only and not the hosted store** (recorded decisions): the hosted P1 store went with encrypted S3 + per-fact DEKs because **provable retraction** was the deciding requirement — shredding a DEK provably destroys a fact, whereas git history retains retracted content. The git-meta backend stays out of hosted production until supersession crypto-shredding exists outside the index. Related known gap (named in purge's caveats): its keep-both merge model has no deletion semantics yet, so privacy purge can't clean it.

content.text:
Got to the bottom of it. Two bugs compose, and yes — **this can hit any team on a connected repo**.

**Bug A — the leak (hosted sync):** `pullHostedFacts` (`internal/cli/hosted_sync.go:306`) runs on your *current git branch*. It pulls the team's fact feed — records stamped `branch:"main"` — and writes them into the current branch's store file **without restamping the branch field** to the store it writes into. The integrity code explicitly documents that invariant ("every writer sets branch to the store it writes into"); this writer violates it. Evidence: every ticket branch we created this session (`cor-2204…`, `cor-2205…`, `cor-2206…`, …) has a store file containing exactly the same 1,517 main-stamped records.

**Bug B — the amplifier (refresh):** `reclassifyAllFactBranches` (`internal/cli/facts_manifest.go:91`, runs on every `refresh`) loads all store files and buckets records **by the branch recorded on the record**, not by file. So main's own file *plus* every leaked copy in the branch files all land in one "main" bucket — concatenated, duplicates and all — and when reclassification touches anything (locus is "always reconciled," so it usually does), it writes that whole bucket back into main's file with no dedup by id. The branch files keep their copies, so the next refresh does it again. That's the geometric growth: the copies-per-id histogram in main's file is almost all exactly 16 and 8 — clean doublings, one per refresh (tonight's refresh took it from 8 to 16; the file's mtime matches the refresh window).

**How we got here:** this repo is connected (background sync every 5 min) and we created ~11 working branches during the audit work. Each branch picked up a full main-fact copy via Bug A; each refresh folded them back into main via Bug B. 1,517 real facts → 38,415 stored main records.

**Exposure:** the preconditions are just "connected repo + feature-branch workflow + refresh" — i.e., the intended usage. Anyone matching that is accumulating duplicates and losing recall; severity arguably higher than most of the audit tickets since it silently corrupts the memory store and the suggested remedy (refresh) makes it worse.

**Proposed plan:**
1. File the ticket with this evidence (High, I'd say).
2. Fix A: restamp (or filter) pulled records to the store's branch; Fix B: dedup by id when rebucketing, or bucket by file.
3. One-time repair path so existing brains converge (dedup keeps first per id — the copies are byte-identical, so it's lossless; your 237 authored memories are unaffected).

input.description:
Found investigating the duplicate-memory-id warning on gh/entireio/entire-brain (2026-10-22). The local brain's facts store grew from 1,517 real facts to 38,415 stored `branch:"main"` records; recall returned empty all week because duplicates shadow memories.

**Two bugs compose**

*Bug A — leak.* `pullHostedFacts` (internal/cli/hosted_sync.go) runs on the current git branch and writes pulled feed records into that branch's store **without restamping `branch`** to the store it writes into. The feed carries the team's facts stamped `branch:"main"`, so every feature branch's store accumulates a full main-stamped copy. This violates the invariant the integrity counter documents ("every writer sets branch to the store it writes into"). Evidence: 11 branch store files each hold exactly the same 1,517 main-stamped records.

*Bug B — amplifier.* `reclassifyAllFactBranches` (internal/cli/facts_manifest.go, runs from every `refresh`) buckets records **by the branch recorded on the record** across ALL store files, then writes the bucket back with no dedup by id. Main's bucket = main's file + every leaked copy → main's file roughly doubles per refresh. Copies-per-id histogram in main's store: 1,310 ids ×16, 177 ×8 — clean doublings, one per refresh.

**Exposure**

Preconditions are the intended usage: connected repo + feature-branch workflow + refresh (manual or watcher). Any such user accumulates duplicates; the integrity warning's own remedy ("run refresh and re-distill") makes it worse.

**Fix**

1. Restamp pulled records to the destination store's branch in `pullHostedFacts`.
2. Make the refresh facts pass operate per store FILE (not per recorded-branch bucket), restamping records to the file's branch and deduping by id — which also self-heals already-damaged brains on their next refresh (the duplicate copies are byte-identical, so repair is lossless).
3. Keep the integrity detection as-is.

content.text:
Full suite running in the background (~10–20 min). While it runs, a summary of the fix now in place on branch `cor-2220-fact-store-duplication`:

- **`factmerge.DedupByID`** — collapses repeated ids through `Upsert`'s existing merge rules (anchor union, newest timestamp, kind/author fill), so repair is lossless even if copies ever diverge.
- **`loadFactStoreFiles`** — new file-level loader; `loadAllFactBranches` (the record-branch view used by 12 read-only consumers) now derives from it, with a comment warning never to write a bucket back into a single file.
- **`reclassifyAllFactBranches`** (the refresh pass) — iterates store *files*, dedups each, writes back in place. This both stops the doubling and **self-heals already-damaged brains on their next refresh** — including anyone else's.
- **Integrity** — duplicates now counted per file (what recall actually reads), so hosted-pull mirrors and `facts promote` copies stop being reported as corruption, while true within-file repeats still warn (existing tests confirm).
- **Deferred deliberately**: restamping pulled records' `branch` field in `pullHostedFacts`. That changes what later gets *pushed* to the hosted set, and the server's branch-upsert semantics live outside this repo — I won't assume them. Noted in COR-2220 as follow-up.

Once the suite is green: commit, PR, then run the fixed binary's refresh against your real brain and verify main's store drops from 22,586 records to 1,517 with the warning gone.

Pushed and answered on the PR. Now the branch-mechanics question — short answer: **mostly no, and your instinct matches the evidence.**

What's actually branch-scoped today:
- **Hosted, the wire connected repos really use** (background sync): fully branchless — the feed and upsert are repo-wide, no branch parameter anywhere.
- **Hosted, legacy/manual wires**: the branch-head CAS (`publish`, `--memories-backend=http`), local-gitmeta (branch is in the key), and the proposals queue are still per-branch.
- **Local**: one store file per branch; recall reads only the current branch's file (defaulting to main when there's no branch).

What per-branch stores still buy: exactly one thing — facts distilled on an experiment branch stay out of main's recall until `facts promote`.

What they cost: because recall sees only the current branch's file, the hosted pull is *forced* to mirror the whole team set into every branch you work on — that mirror is the root enabler of COR-2220; plus ~12 redundant copies of the team set on disk across 57 store dirs, inflated fact counts, facts stranded on deleted branches when nobody runs `promote`, and a `branch` field that means two different things (where it was distilled vs. which store holds it).

So the defensible end-state is: **one repo-level store + a small "pending" partition for unpromoted branch-local distills**, with branch kept as a provenance field only. That kills the mirror, the duplication bug class, and most of the promote ceremony. But it's a real migration — store layout, recall, promote/review/gc, publish, gitmeta keys, manifest schema — a design ticket, not something to bolt onto #438.

input.title: Design: collapse per-branch fact stores to one repo-level store + pending partition
input.description:
Follow-up to COR-2220, where the per-branch store layout was the root enabler of the duplication bug.

**Current state**

- The hosted wire connected repos actually use (background per-fact feed, COR-2126) is repo-wide and branchless: `FactsFeedPage(repoID)`, `UpsertFacts(repoID)`.
- Branch scoping survives in: local per-branch store files (`facts/<slug>-<hash>/facts.ndjson`), recall (reads only the current branch's file, default main), the branch-head CAS wire (`publish`, `--memories-backend=http`), local-gitmeta keys, and the proposals queue.
- The only behavior per-branch stores still buy locally: facts distilled on a branch stay out of main's recall until `facts promote`.

**Costs of keeping it**

- Because recall sees only the current branch's file, the hosted pull must mirror the whole team set into every working branch — the mirror that enabled COR-2220, and the reason `pullHostedFacts` writes main-stamped records into other stores (the restamp question deferred on COR-2220 is subsumed here).
- ~12 redundant copies of the team set across 57 store dirs on this repo; inflated fact counts in status/manifest.
- Branch-local facts strand when branches are deleted without `promote`.
- The record `branch` field means two things at once: where the fact was distilled vs. which store holds it.

**Proposed end-state**

One repo-level store, plus a small "pending" partition for unpromoted branch-local distills (replacing per-branch files); `branch` becomes provenance metadata only. Kills the mirror, the duplication bug class, and most of the promote ceremony.

**Migration surface**

Store layout + one-time migration, recall/evidence source, distill write path, promote/review/gc, publish + branch-head CAS semantics, local-gitmeta keys, manifest schema (`branches`, counts), integrity accounting. Decide what branch scoping (if any) the CAS/proposals wires keep.

but the existing released binary still works as expected, right?

Yes, with precise boundaries:

**For users who only have the released binary** — it behaves exactly as it did when released. Nothing we merged changes anything on their machines until they upgrade. That includes the bad part: the released binary *contains* the COR-2220 bug, so on connected repos it keeps duplicating fact stores and degrading recall — that's the "expected" behavior it shipped with, and it heals automatically on the first refresh after they upgrade.

**The failure I hit tonight is only the mixed-version case**: a machine where a *newer* build has written the brain manifest (it adds a `suppressed_warnings` field), and then the *older* binary runs a mutating command. The old binary fails closed — deliberately and with a clear message — rather than silently dropping the field on rewrite; read-only commands still work, and the brain file itself is explicitly not damaged. Released users can't be in this state; only dev machines (like mine) that ran a main build alongside the installed plugin are.

**Downgrade is the one rough edge**: if someone upgrades, then rolls back to the released binary, its writes will refuse until a `refresh --force` rebuilds the manifest. Worth a line in the release notes if rollback is a supported path.

So: release-safe. Old binary reads everything the new one writes, fails closed instead of corrupting on writes it doesn't understand, and the new build repairs the old build's damage on arrival.
so is it fair to say in all cases then a refresh --force resolves any issues? in mixed and old binaries?

Not quite — it's fair for the mixed case, wrong for the old-binary case, and unnecessary for the new one:

- **New binary (post-release)**: plain `refresh` resolves everything, `--force` never needed. The heal is built into the normal path — that's the property we validated.
- **Mixed / downgrade** (new build wrote the manifest, old binary running): yes — `refresh --force` is the escape hatch, and it's what the old binary's own error message prescribes. Two caveats: it works by *erasing* the newer build's extra manifest data (that's exactly why the old binary refuses without `--force`), and I haven't executed it myself — I'm relaying the binary's documented remedy, not a tested result.
- **Old binary alone**: no. Refresh — forced or not — is the thing *causing* the duplication there; running it more makes the store worse, never better. The only resolution for old binaries is upgrading, after which the first plain refresh heals the accumulated damage.

So the release-notes framing would be: "upgrade, then refresh" fixes everything; `refresh --force` is only the rollback escape hatch; nothing fixes the old binary in place.

I checked rather than assumed, and the honest answer is: **that guarantee cannot be delivered to an old binary — but the exposed population is small and bounded, and here's the full picture.**

**What the code says:**
- The amplifier runs from one place, `runRefresh` — and the **watch daemon's 5-minute tick calls that same function** (`watch.go:721`). So old binaries don't need a manual refresh to duplicate; a healthy watcher on a connected repo can do it on its own. (We survived this week partly by luck — your daemon was wedged.) One mitigating detail: the old code only rewrites a store when reclassification finds something to change, so ticks over an already-settled store don't double; it's new/unreconciled facts that re-trigger it.
- Neither bug is reachable server-side: the amplifier never touches the network, and the feed API doesn't know the client's branch, so we can't patch old clients from the server in any clean way.

**Who's actually on "the old binary":**
- There is no stable release — only **nightlies**. The leak shipped **2026-10-07** (`hostedFactsSyncAndPull`), and connect is gated (trail-memories flag, CLI ≥ 0.11.6). So the exposed set is: people on a nightly from the last ~2 weeks **and** connected — essentially the team, not a long tail of frozen users. Nightly users roll forward by default, and the first refresh on the fixed build heals all accumulated damage.

**So for the release:**
1. The real action is making sure the team's installed plugins update promptly (that *is* the "old binary" population today).
2. If you ever do need to protect clients that genuinely won't upgrade, the only lever I found is server-side: normalize the `branch` field on feed records so an old client's cross-file "main" bucket can't form. That's entire-api surgery with side effects I can't verify from this repo — I'd scope it on COR-2221 only if a frozen-client population actually materializes.

what is cor-2211?

COR-2211 is the one open *decision* from the audit: **should plain `entire brain memories sync` use the hosted backend on a connected repo?**

Today, `memories sync` with no flags always syncs via **local-gitmeta** (the on-disk git store — fully local, no network), even when the repo is connected. Hosted sync only happens if you explicitly pass `--memories-backend=http`. The audit flagged that this might surprise a user on a connected repo who runs `memories sync` meaning "sync with my team."

What's already done (PR #435, merged + validated): the command's help now states this plainly — local-gitmeta is the default, connecting the repo doesn't change it, `--memories-backend=http` opts into hosted.

What's left — your call between:
- **Keep the local default** (the recommendation): hosted sync already happens automatically via the background per-fact wire on connected repos, so a hosted default for the manual command would be redundant — and it would route manual sync through a *different* wire (branch-head CAS + proposals) with different conflict semantics. It also preserves the ADR-P1-A rule that connect state never silently turns a local command into network egress.
- **Switch when connected**: matches the "sync means team sync" intuition, but needs the wire choice, env-precedence rules, and escape hatches designed first (sketched in the PR body).

Closing the ticket accepts keep-local; nothing else to do in that case. If you lean switch, it becomes a small design task. Given the ADR and the redundancy argument, I'd close it as keep-local.

- `entire brain remember "<rule>" --path <topic>` — saves decisions or lessons with topic grouping
- `entire brain recall "<topic>"` — looks up saved facts (use for saved information vs. broader search)
- `entire brain inspect impact <symbol>` — with Entire Graph installed, shows impact of changing code
- `entire brain inspect changes` — inspects changes since last index
- `entire brain status --verbose` — shows available, missing, or outdated sources
- `entire brain verify` — checks whether saved facts still reference matching sources

**Key Claims:**

Brain helps users "find earlier decisions, save lessons, and give your agent context before it starts work." The `query` command "combines keyword and meaning-based search" by default. Hand-entered facts may show `unverifiable-here` status. Verification "checks references, not whether a fact is correct."

# entire-graph for Coding Agents

## Core Capability

The documentation explains how to leverage entire-graph with your coding agent. Rather than running commands yourself, you can ask your agent questions about the repository, and it will select the appropriate entire-graph operation.

## Supported Operations

The system maps natural language queries to specific commands:

| Objective | Sample Question | Corresponding Operation |
| - | - | - |
| Locate code | Where is request routing implemented? | `search` |
| Explain implementation | Show and explain the definition of `ResolveRoute`. | `def` |
| Find relationships | What calls `ResolveRoute`? | `neighbors` |
| Evaluate consequences | What could be affected if I change `ResolveRoute`? | `impact` |
| Analyze changes | Summarize the semantic changes from `main` to `HEAD`. | `diff` |
| Extract structure | Export the repository graph as NDJSON. | `snapshot` |

## Agent Workflow

"For a task that requires finding code, your agent starts with a entire-graph search to narrow its investigation. It then reads the source around the most relevant results and uses follow-up entire-graph queries when it needs to trace relationships or assess impact."

The documentation emphasizes that "entire-graph returns evidence for your agent to check, not a final conclusion."

## Key Limitation

"If a task already identifies the exact file and the file is small, your agent can read it directly. entire-graph is most useful when your agent needs to find where to begin or understand how code connects."

--verify-block off (or --omit-verify, or ENTIRE_GRAPH_VERIFY_BLOCK=off) removes the VERIFY block and nothing else: the test command and the run-once/fix/stop advice that rides with it. That advice would help an agent with no tool just as much, so it exists for fair A/B comparisons (both arms get it, or neither). JSON then omits verify_command and reports stats.verify_omitted. In agent format the freed bytes go to ranked results under the same --max-context-bytes, so off is a different selection, not the on payload with lines deleted.
--top-k caps normal results, including automatic related sites and covering tests, without changing retrieval strategy. Explicit --callee-hop may add called-helper results beyond that cap, under its existing byte-budget and ranked-source protections. --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).
Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.
